summary.text: Using \(kB_N(k)=N E_N(k)\), the summand is rewritten integrally as \(T_N(k)=B_N(k)^2(B_N(k)+2E_N(k))\), and the indices are split into multiples and nonmultiples of \(p\); a rising-factorial factorization into its \(p\)-divisible part and \(p\)-unit product, together with the divisibility of \(B_N(k)\), gives the required termwise congruence at multiples of \(p\). At nonmultiples, only a leading inverse-square term remains modulo \(p^{3r}\), and its sum vanishes in blocks because reciprocal squares sum to zero modulo powers of \(p\); multiplication by \(2\) permutes the residue ring, while pairing \(j\) with \(L-j\) supplies the stronger first-harmonic estimate used in the product expansion.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(N)=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N}(N+2k)\binom{N+k-1}{k}^{3}
\qquad (N\geq 1).
\]
We prove that, for every prime \(p\geq5\), every \(n\geq1\), and every \(r\geq1\),
\[
a(np^r)\equiv a(np^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r}}.
\]

Throughout the proof we work in the ring \(\mathbb Z_p\) of \(p\)-adic integers. For \(x\in\mathbb Z_p\), write
\[
D_e(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p^e\mid x
\]
in \(\mathbb Z_p\). The usual rules will be used freely: sums of elements satisfying \(D_e\) again satisfy \(D_e\); if \(D_e(x)\) and \(D_f(y)\), then \(D_{e+f}(xy)\); and \(D_f(x)\) implies \(D_e(x)\) when \(e\leq f\). For an ordinary integer \(m\), \(D_e(m)\) is equivalent to the ordinary divisibility \(p^e\mid m\).

Define a modified reciprocal
\[
\iota(j)=
\begin{cases}
j^{-1}&p\nmid j,\\
0&p\mid j,
\end{cases}
\qquad \iota(j)\in\mathbb Z_p.
\]
Thus \(j\iota(j)=1\) if \(p\nmid j\), while all terms whose denominator would be divisible by \(p\) are simply omitted by being assigned value zero.

We first establish the harmonic-sum estimates needed later.

### 1. Reciprocal-square sums

For every \(e\geq0\) and every integer \(A\geq0\),
\[
D_e\left(\sum_{j=0}^{p^e-1}\iota(A+j)^2\right).
\tag{1}
\]
Indeed, reduce the sum modulo \(p^e\). The residues \(A,A+1,\ldots,A+p^e-1\) run through all of \(\mathbb Z/p^e\mathbb Z\), so it is enough to prove
\[
\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z/p^e\mathbb Z}\iota(x)^2=0.
\]
Multiplication by \(2\) permutes this finite ring. Since \(2\) is a unit, modified inversion satisfies \(\iota(2x)=2^{-1}\iota(x)\), including when \(x\) is a nonunit. Therefore, if the displayed sum is \(S\), reindexing by \(x\mapsto2x\) gives
\[
S=2^{-2}S.
\]
Hence \(3S=0\), after multiplication by the unit \(4\). Since \(p\geq5\), \(3\) is also a unit modulo \(p^e\), and consequently \(S=0\). This proves (1).

By dividing an interval into consecutive blocks of length \(p^e\), we immediately obtain: whenever \(p^e\mid L\),
\[
D_e\left(\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}\iota(A+j)^2\right).
\tag{2}
\]

We also need a stronger estimate for reciprocal first powers. If \(s>0\) and \(p^s\mid L\), then
\[
D_{2s}\left(\sum_{j=0}^{L}\iota(j)\right).
\tag{3}
\]
To prove this, first note that \(p\mid L\). Pair \(j\) with \(L-j\). For every \(0\leq j\leq L\),
\[
\iota(j)+\iota(L-j)=L\iota(j)\iota(L-j).
\tag{4}
\]
If \(p\mid j\), then \(p\mid L-j\), and both sides are zero. Otherwise both \(j\) and \(L-j\) are units, and (4) is just
\(1/j+1/(L-j)=L/(j(L-j))\).

A useful rearrangement of (4), obtained by multiplying it by \(1+L\iota(j)\), is
\[
\iota(j)+\iota(L-j)
 =L^2\iota(j)^2\iota(L-j)-L\iota(j)^2.
\]
Summing over \(j=0,\ldots,L\), and observing that reflection \(j\mapsto L-j\) leaves the reciprocal sum unchanged, gives
\[
2\sum_{j=0}^{L}\iota(j)
=L^2\sum_{j=0}^{L}\iota(j)^2\iota(L-j)
-L\sum_{j=0}^{L}\iota(j)^2.
\tag{5}
\]
Now \(D_s(L)\), hence \(D_{2s}(L^2)\). Also, by (2),
\[
D_s\left(\sum_{j=0}^{L}\iota(j)^2\right),
\]
because the endpoint term \(\iota(L)^2\) vanishes and the remaining interval has length \(L\). Thus both terms on the right of (5) are divisible by \(p^{2s}\). Since \(2\) is a \(p\)-adic unit, (3) follows.

### 2. A rising-factorial product

For nonnegative integers \(N,L\), define
\[
U(N,L)=\prod_{j=0}^{L}\bigl(1+N\iota(j)\bigr).
\tag{6}
\]
The factor for \(j=0\), and more generally every factor with \(p\mid j\), is \(1\). Thus this is the part of the usual rising-factorial quotient contributed by denominators prime to \(p\).

We use the following elementary product expansion. Suppose each \(x_i\) is divisible by \(p^r\), and put
\[
P=\prod_i(1+x_i),\qquad H=\sum_i x_i,
\qquad Q=\sum_i x_i^2.
\]
Then
\[
D_r(P-1),
\tag{7}
\]
\[
D_{2r}(P-1-H),
\tag{8}
\]
and
\[
D_{3r}(2P-2-2H-H^2+Q).
\tag{9}
\]
These statements follow by expanding the product according to degree. Equation (7) says every nonconstant monomial has degree at least one; (8), after subtracting the linear terms, says every remaining monomial has degree at least two. For (9), observe that
\((H^2-Q)/2\) is exactly the sum of all products \(x_ix_j\) with \(i\ne j\); hence the displayed expression has no terms of degrees zero, one, or two, and all its remaining terms have degree at least three. This argument is valid integrally without dividing by \(2\), as reflected by the factor \(2\) in (9).

The basic consequence is that if \(p^r\mid N\), then
\[
D_r(U(N,L)-1).
\tag{10}
\]
More importantly, suppose
\[
p^r\mid N,\qquad p^s\mid L,
\qquad 0\leq s\leq r.
\]
Then
\[
D_{r+2s}(U(N,L)-1).
\tag{11}
\]
For \(s=0\), this is just (10). Assume \(s>0\), and apply (7)–(9) to
\(x_j=N\iota(j)\), \(0\leq j\leq L\). In this notation
\[
H=N\sum_{j=0}^{L}\iota(j),
\qquad
Q=N^2\sum_{j=0}^{L}\iota(j)^2.
\]
By (3), \(D_{r+2s}(H)\). By (2), the reciprocal-square sum is divisible by \(p^s\), so \(Q\) is divisible by \(p^{2r+s}\), hence by \(p^{r+2s}\) because \(s\leq r\). The expression in (9) is divisible by \(p^{3r}\), hence by \(p^{r+2s}\). Finally,
\[
2(U-1)=
(2U-2-2H-H^2+Q)+2H+H^2-Q.
\]
Every term on the right is divisible by \(p^{r+2s}\). Since \(2\) is a unit, (11) follows.

### 3. Splitting binomial coefficients

Put
\[
C(N,k)=\binom{N+k}{k}.
\]
The basic recurrence is
\[
(k+1)C(N,k+1)=(N+k+1)C(N,k).
\tag{12}
\]
We claim that in \(\mathbb Z_p\),
\[
C(pn,k)=C\left(n,\left\lfloor\frac{k}{p}\right\rfloor\right)U(pn,k).
\tag{13}
\]
This follows by induction on \(k\) using (12). When passing from \(k\) to \(k+1\), there are two cases. If \(p\nmid k+1\), then \(\lfloor(k+1)/p\rfloor=\lfloor k/p\rfloor\), and the new factor in \(U\) is
\[
1+pn\iota(k+1)=\frac{pn+k+1}{k+1},
\]
which is exactly the quotient dictated by (12). If \(p\mid k+1\), the new factor in \(U\) is \(1\), while the floor increases by one; recurrence (12) for \(C(n,\cdot)\), after cancelling the common factor \(p\), gives precisely the required change. This proves (13).

Combining (13) with (10), we get the approximation
\[
p^r\mid pn
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
D_r\left(C(pn,k)-C\left(n,\left\lfloor\frac{k}{p}\right\rfloor\right)\right).
\tag{14}
\]
The same congruence remains true after taking any fixed positive power, because \(x-y\mid x^d-y^d\).

We next record a weighted harmonic consequence of (14). If \(p^s\mid L\), and functions \(f,g:\mathbb N\to\mathbb Z_p\) satisfy
\(D_r(f(t)-g(t))\) for every \(t\), then
\[
D_{s+r}\left(
\sum_{k=0}^{L-1}
\left(f\left(\left\lfloor\frac{k}{p^s}\right\rfloor\right)
-g\left(\left\lfloor\frac{k}{p^s}\right\rfloor\right)\right)
\iota(k)^2\right).
\tag{15}
\]
Indeed, divide \(0,\ldots,L-1\) into blocks of length \(p^s\). The coefficient \(f(t)-g(t)\) is constant on each block and is divisible by \(p^r\), while the reciprocal-square sum on that block is divisible by \(p^s\) by (1).

Iterating (15) gives the key weighted estimate:
\[
p^{s+r}\mid L
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
D_{s+r}\left(
\sum_{k=0}^{L-1}
C\left(np^r,\left\lfloor\frac{k}{p^s}\right\rfloor\right)^3
\iota(k)^2\right).
\tag{16}
\]
Here is the full induction on \(r\). If \(r=0\), divide the interval into blocks of length \(p^s\). On each block the binomial coefficient is constant, and (1) makes the reciprocal-square sum divisible by \(p^s\).

For the induction step, compare
\[
C\left(np^{r+1},t\right)^3
\quad\text{with}\quad
C\left(np^r,\left\lfloor\frac t p\right\rfloor\right)^3.
\]
By (14), their difference is divisible by \(p^{r+1}\). Formula (15), with block size \(p^s\), shows that replacing the first coefficient by the second changes the weighted sum by a multiple of \(p^{s+r+1}\). But
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor k/p^s\rfloor}{p}\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor\frac{k}{p^{s+1}}\right\rfloor,
\]
and the remaining sum is divisible by \(p^{(s+1)+r}\) by the induction hypothesis with \(s+1\) in place of \(s\). This proves (16).

### 4. Integral summands

Define
\[
B(N,k)=\binom{N+k-1}{N-1},
\qquad
E(N,k)=\binom{N+k-1}{N},
\]
and
\[
T(N,k)=B(N,k)^2\bigl(B(N,k)+2E(N,k)\bigr).
\tag{17}
\]
For \(N>0\), Pascal's identity and the standard adjacent-binomial identity give
\[
C(N,k)=B(N,k)+E(N,k),
\tag{18}
\]
\[
kB(N,k)=NE(N,k).
\tag{19}
\]
In particular,
\[
(N+k)B(N,k)=NC(N,k).
\tag{20}
\]
Also \(B(N,0)=1\), \(E(N,0)=0\), and therefore \(T(N,0)=1\).

At indices divisible by \(p\), (13), (18), and (20) imply
\[
B(pn,pk)=B(n,k)U(pn,pk),
\qquad
E(pn,pk)=E(n,k)U(pn,pk).
\tag{21}
\]
For the first identity, (13) gives \(C(pn,pk)=C(n,k)U(pn,pk)\); substituting this into (20) for \((pn,pk)\) and comparing with (20) for \((n,k)\) gives the formula for \(B\). The formula for \(E\) then follows from (18). Consequently,
\[
T(pn,pk)=T(n,k)U(pn,pk)^3.
\tag{22}
\]

At an index prime to \(p\), (19) gives
\[
B(N,k)=N\iota(k)E(N,k).
\tag{23}
\]
If \(p^r\mid pn\) and \(p\nmid k\), then, using
\(E(pn,k)=C(pn,k-1)\) and (14),
\[
E(pn,k)\equiv C\left(n,\left\lfloor\frac{k}{p}\right\rfloor\right)
\pmod {p^r}.
\tag{24}
\]
(The floor is unchanged when one replaces \(k\) by \(k-1\), because \(p\nmid k\).)

Substituting (23) into (17) yields
\[
T(pn,k)
=(pn)^3\iota(k)^3E(pn,k)^3
+2(pn)^2\iota(k)^2E(pn,k)^3.
\]
The first term is divisible by \(p^{3r}\), and (24), cubed, may be used in the second term because its prefactor is already divisible by \(p^{2r}\). Hence, for \(p\nmid k\),
\[
T(pn,k)\equiv
2(pn)^2\iota(k)^2
C\left(n,\left\lfloor\frac{k}{p}\right\rfloor\right)^3
\pmod {p^{3r}}.
\tag{25}
\]

### 5. Terms at multiples of \(p\)

Suppose now that \(r\geq1\), \(n>0\), and
\[
p^{r-1}\mid n.
\tag{26}
\]
Then \(p^r\mid pn\). We claim that for every \(k\geq0\),
\[
T(pn,pk)\equiv T(n,k)\pmod {p^{3r}}.
\tag{27}
\]
For \(k=0\), both sides equal \(1\). If \(k>0\), write
\[
k=p^tu,\qquad p\nmid u.
\]
By (22), the difference in (27) is
\[
T(n,k)\bigl(U(pn,pk)^3-1\bigr).
\tag{28}
\]
Since \(pk=p^{t+1}u\), estimate (11) applies.

If \(r\leq t+1\), use \(s=r\) in (11). It gives
\[
U(pn,pk)\equiv1\pmod {p^{3r}},
\]
and therefore also \(U(pn,pk)^3\equiv1\pmod {p^{3r}}\). Thus (28) has the desired divisibility.

It remains to consider \(t+1<r\). From (19), together with (26), one obtains
\[
D_{r-1-t}(B(n,p^tu)).
\tag{29}
\]
Indeed, \(p^{r-1}\) divides the right side \(nE(n,k)\) of (19); on the left side, cancelling \(p^t\) and then the unit \(u\) leaves exactly (29). Since \(T\) contains the factor \(B^2\),
\[
D_{2(r-t-1)}(T(n,k)).
\tag{30}
\]
On the other hand, (11) with \(s=t+1\) gives
\[
D_{r+2(t+1)}(U(pn,pk)-1),
\]
and hence the same divisibility for \(U(pn,pk)^3-1\). Combining this with (30), the exponent in (28) is at least
\[
2(r-t-1)+r+2(t+1)=3r.
\]
This proves (27) in all cases.

### 6. Cancellation of the indices not divisible by \(p\)

Still under (26), sum (25) over \(0\leq k\leq pn\) with \(p\nmid k\). Terms with \(p\mid k\) may be inserted into the right-hand sum because \(\iota(k)=0\). The endpoint \(k=pn\) also contributes zero. Thus the required model sum is
\[
2(pn)^2
\sum_{k=0}^{pn-1}
C\left(n,\left\lfloor\frac{k}{p}\right\rfloor\right)^3\iota(k)^2.
\tag{31}
\]
Apply (16) with \(s=1\), with its exponent parameter equal to \(r-1\), and with \(L=pn\). The assumptions hold because \(p^{r-1}\mid n\), so \(p^r\mid pn\). It follows that the sum in (31) is divisible by \(p^r\). The prefactor \((pn)^2\) is divisible by \(p^{2r}\). Therefore (31) is divisible by \(p^{3r}\).

Together with the termwise congruence (25), this proves
\[
\sum_{\substack{0\leq k\leq pn\\p\nmid k}}T(pn,k)
\equiv0\pmod {p^{3r}}.
\tag{32}
\]

Define
\[
F(N)=\sum_{k=0}^{N}T(N,k).
\]
The multiples of \(p\) in \(0,\ldots,pn\) are exactly \(pk\) for \(0\leq k\leq n\). Summing (27) over those indices and adding (32) gives
\[
F(pn)\equiv F(n)\pmod {p^{3r}}
\quad\text{whenever }p^{r-1}\mid n.
\tag{33}
\]

### 7. Identification with the original sequence

It remains to show that \(F(N)=a(N)\). Since
\[
B(N,k)=\binom{N+k-1}{N-1}=\binom{N+k-1}{k},
\]
equation (19) gives, term by term,
\[
\begin{aligned}
(N+2k)B(N,k)^3
&=NB(N,k)^3+2\,kB(N,k)\,B(N,k)^2\\
&=N B(N,k)^3+2N E(N,k)B(N,k)^2\\
&=N T(N,k).
\end{aligned}
\]
Summing and dividing by the positive integer \(N\), we obtain
\[
a(N)=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N}(N+2k)B(N,k)^3
=\sum_{k=0}^{N}T(N,k)=F(N).
\tag{34}
\]
This also directly proves that the quotient defining \(a(N)\) is integral.

Finally set
\[
m=np^{r-1}.
\]
Then \(m>0\), \(p^{r-1}\mid m\), and, since \(r\geq1\),
\[
pm=np^r.
\]
Applying (33) to \(m\), and then using (34), yields
\[
a(np^r)=F(pm)\equiv F(m)=a(np^{r-1})
\pmod {p^{3r}}.
\]
This is the desired supercongruence.
